## Website Designer in Pune: What a Business Website Costs in 2026 and What Drives the Price

A website designer in Pune will typically quote anywhere from the low tens of thousands of rupees for a simple brochure site on a template, to several lakhs for a custom-designed, content-heavy or integrated site, and well beyond that for a custom-built web application. The spread is wide because "a website" is not one product. The price follows four things: how many unique page designs you need, whether the build is template-based or custom, how much functionality sits behind the pages, and who writes and prepares the content. If you understand those four levers, you can read any quotation and see what you are actually buying.

This article is for a business owner, practice manager or marketing head in Pune who has two or three quotes on the table that differ by a factor of five and cannot tell why. It explains what is normally included in each tier, what is usually left out, where money gets spent without being noticed, and how to ask for a quote that can be compared line by line. The rupee ranges below are indicative planning ranges for the Indian market, not a rate card; they will move with scope, and the only number that matters for your project is the written one you receive after a proper brief.

### Why quotes for "a website" differ so much

Imagine asking three builders for "a house". One quotes a one-room structure, one a two-bedroom flat, one a bungalow with a garden. All are houses. Website quotes behave the same way because the brief is usually a sentence: "We need a website for our company, about eight pages."

Behind that sentence sit decisions nobody has made yet. Do the eight pages share two layouts or have eight different designs? Is the text written, or does the designer write it? Do you need a blog, a contact form that feeds a CRM, a booking calendar, a product catalogue? Will the site be edited by your staff afterwards? Is it expected to rank on Google, which means technical SEO groundwork, or merely to exist as an online brochure?

Each unanswered question gets answered silently by whoever writes the quote, and they answer differently. That is the real reason for a 5x spread. The fix is not to find the cheapest quote; it is to remove the silent assumptions before you ask.

### The four price levers

#### Lever 1: Unique designs, not page count

A designer does not charge per page so much as per *unique layout*. A twenty-page site with one home design, one inner-page design and one service-page template is less work than a ten-page site where every page is a bespoke composition. When you ask for a quote, list pages grouped by type: home, about, services (how many, and do they share a layout), blog, contact, legal pages. A quote that says "up to 10 pages" without saying how many designs exist is hiding the thing that drives the cost.

#### Lever 2: Template or custom design

A template-based website starts from a pre-built theme and is customised with your logo, colours, images and content. It is quicker and cheaper, and for many small businesses it is entirely adequate. A custom design starts from your brand and your goals: wireframes, a visual design usually produced in a tool such as Figma, and then a build that matches it. It costs more because there is more skilled work in it, and it pays off when the website has to do something specific, differentiate you in a crowded category, or carry a brand that a template cannot express.

Neither is "better". A dentist's clinic with one location and four treatments may be well served by a clean, fast, template-based WordPress site. A manufacturer launching a distributor portal or a brand with a distinctive identity usually needs custom design. Be wary of any quote that calls a template "custom" without being specific about what was designed from scratch.

#### Lever 3: Functionality behind the pages

The most expensive part of many websites is not what visitors see but what happens when they click. Typical functionality, roughly from cheapest to most expensive to build well:

- A contact form that emails you.
- A contact form that also saves enquiries to a CRM and sends an acknowledgement.
- A WhatsApp click-to-chat button and a floating chat widget.
- Online appointment or enquiry scheduling.
- A multilingual site (English plus Marathi or Hindi), which multiplies content and testing work.
- A product catalogue without checkout.
- A full ecommerce store with payment gateway, shipping and order management.
- A member login area, client portal or donation platform with receipts and reports.

Each step up adds design, development, testing and ongoing maintenance. This is the point at which a "website" shades into a web application and the quote should be treated differently, with a written specification rather than a page list.

#### Lever 4: Content and assets

Many projects are delayed and over budget not because of design but because of content. Who writes the text? Who photographs the office, the team or the products? Who creates the logo if you lack one? A designer who includes "content" in a quote may mean they will place your text into the design, not write it. Clarify three things in writing: copywriting (is it included, for how many pages, with how many revisions), photography and imagery (stock, supplied or shot), and logo and brand assets.

### What a typical quotation should contain

A comparable quote lists, at the least:

- **Scope:** the pages and page types, and the number of unique designs.
- **Design approach:** template or custom, the number of concepts and rounds of revision.
- **Functionality:** every form, integration, plugin and third-party tool, named.
- **Content:** who writes, who supplies images, and how much is included.
- **Technical groundwork:** mobile responsiveness, page speed targets, basic on-page SEO (titles, descriptions, headings, image alt text), redirects if replacing an old site, analytics and Search Console set-up, SSL.
- **Platform and ownership:** WordPress, Shopify, custom code; who owns the code, design files and domain; what happens if you leave.
- **Timeline:** with milestones and your approval points.
- **Post-launch:** a support or warranty period, and what it covers.
- **Exclusions:** the things not included. A good quote is as clear about these as about the inclusions.

If the quote is a single line with a single number, it can be compared with nothing. Ask for the breakdown.

### Indicative ranges by type of website

The figures below are planning ranges only, reflecting how projects of each type are commonly scoped in India. They exclude GST, domain, hosting, premium plugin licences, paid stock images and any content writing unless stated. Expect real quotes to fall outside them if your requirements are unusual.

#### A simple brochure site (3 to 8 pages, template-based)

For a small business that needs a credible web presence: home, about, services, contact and perhaps a gallery. Template-based, mobile-responsive, a contact form, basic SEO set-up. Budget in the range of tens of thousands of rupees. The risk to watch is a site that looks fine but is slow, has no analytics, and has no way for you to edit it later.

#### A custom-designed business website (8 to 20 pages)

For a business where the website is part of how it wins clients: professional services, healthcare groups, manufacturers, schools, B2B companies. Custom visual design, multiple page templates, a blog or news section, integrations such as CRM or WhatsApp, and proper technical SEO. Budget commonly runs from a lakh or two into the lower lakhs, rising with the number of templates and integrations. This is where the difference between a real brief and a vague one has the largest effect on the price.

#### An ecommerce website

Because ecommerce adds catalogue, checkout, tax-ready invoices, shipping integration and order management, it is priced separately from a business website. A small Shopify or WooCommerce store with a modest catalogue is quoted very differently from a store with hundreds of variants, multiple payment and shipping integrations and custom features. For that category see our guide to [ecommerce website development in Pune](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-guide-2026), which compares platforms and cost drivers.

#### An NGO or donation website

NGO sites carry functions most business sites do not: online donation, recurring giving, 80G receipts, donor databases and reporting. Pricing is shaped by those features. We have covered ranges in detail in [NGO Website Cost in India](/blog/ngo-website-cost-india-complete-guide), and our [NGO website service](/pages/ngopage/) page describes what is included.

#### A custom web application

Portals, dashboards, booking engines, marketplaces and anything where users log in and do things are software projects, not website projects. Quote these from a written specification, with phased milestones, and treat the figure as an estimate with a change process rather than a fixed price.

### The costs that are not in the design quote

A quotation for design and development is only part of what a website costs in its first year. Budget separately for:

- **Domain name:** an annual renewal, usually modest.
- **Hosting:** shared hosting is the cheapest; managed WordPress or cloud hosting costs more and is usually faster and better supported. See our note on [choosing WordPress hosting in India](/blog/choose-wordpress-hosting-india).
- **Premium themes and plugins:** many are annual licences. Ask which ones your site depends on and who pays for renewals.
- **Content:** copywriting, photography, video, translation.
- **Third-party tools:** email service, CRM, booking software, chat, analytics.
- **Maintenance:** security updates, backups, uptime monitoring, small content changes. See our guide on [website maintenance and support in Pune](/blog/website-maintenance-support-pune-guide-2026).
- **Marketing:** a website does not generate leads by existing. SEO, Google Ads or social media is a separate budget.

A rule of thumb many agencies use is that maintenance and running costs for a live site are a modest percentage of the build per year, but because that percentage depends heavily on the platform and what is installed, ask for it in writing rather than assuming.

### Red flags in a website design quote

- **A fixed low price with no scope.** If you cannot see what is included, it will be added to later.
- **"Unlimited" revisions or pages.** Nobody can deliver unlimited anything. Ask what happens when you hit the real limit.
- **No mention of ownership.** You should own the design files, the content and, where possible, the code. A designer who retains ownership of your site can make leaving expensive.
- **Heavy page builders and many plugins by default.** They can make a site slow and harder to maintain. See our comparison of [WordPress themes versus page builders](/blog/wordpress-theme-vs-page-builder).
- **No testing or staging.** Sites should be tested on real phones and browsers before launch, not only on the designer's laptop.
- **SEO described as "SEO-friendly" with nothing specific.** Ask what that means: titles, descriptions, headings, speed, redirects, sitemap.
- **A guaranteed Google ranking.** Nobody controls rankings. A guarantee is a sign to leave.
- **Everything paid upfront.** Staged payments tied to milestones protect both sides.

### How to compare three quotes properly

Do not compare the totals. Build a simple table, one column per designer, and one row for each item below. Fill it in from the quotes and mark anything missing.

1. Pages and unique designs.
2. Template or custom.
3. Functionality and integrations, each named.
4. Content: writing, images, logo.
5. Technical SEO and speed.
6. Platform and ownership.
7. Timeline and milestones.
8. Support period after launch.
9. Items excluded.
10. Payment schedule.

When a row is blank for one designer and filled for another, that is where the price difference lives. Send the table back to every designer and ask them to complete it. The quotes that come back will be comparable, and the conversation is usually more honest.

### A worked example: a clinic group in Pune

To make this concrete, consider an illustrative case, not a client: a clinic with two branches wants a new website. The first quote is a template-based site with five pages, a contact form and a WhatsApp button. The second is a custom design with a page per treatment, a booking form that feeds a CRM, a Marathi version and a blog, plus local SEO set-up including a page for each branch.

They are not competing for the same job. The first is a presence; the second is a patient-acquisition system. The right decision depends on the clinic's goals: if most patients come through referrals and Google Business Profile and the site is a confirmation step, the first may be enough. If the clinic wants to rank for treatment searches in Pune and capture appointment requests at all hours, the second is closer to what is needed. Where the price difference is large, ask the cheaper designer what is *not* in their quote, and ask the dearer one which items could be deferred to a second phase.

Phasing is the most underused way to manage cost. A site that launches with the core pages and the integrations that matter, and adds a blog, a second language or a booking system after three months, spreads the spend and lets real visitor behaviour shape the later work.

### Fixed price, time and materials, or retainer

Most business websites are quoted at a fixed price against an agreed scope. That works when the scope is clear. For projects with uncertainty, such as a web application, a time-and-materials or phased arrangement is more honest: you pay for effort in stages with a cap you can review. For post-launch work, a monthly retainer for maintenance and small updates is usually cheaper than ad-hoc requests, provided the retainer states the hours and what they cover.

Whichever you choose, agree how changes will be handled. Scope changes are normal. A written change process (describe the change, estimate the effort, approve, then do it) prevents disputes later.

### Questions to ask before you sign

1. Who will design and who will develop my site, and can I see work by those people?
2. Is the design template-based or custom, and what exactly will be custom?
3. Who owns the final design files, code and content?
4. What is included in post-launch support and for how long?
5. How will you protect existing search rankings if you are replacing a site? (See our guide on [website redesign versus rebuild](/blog/website-redesign-vs-rebuild-pune-2026).)
6. How will the site be tested for mobile devices and speed?
7. What will I need to supply, and by when, to keep the timeline?
8. What is not included?

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much does a website designer in Pune charge?

It depends on scope, not city. A simple template-based brochure site is at the lower end, a custom-designed business website costs more, and ecommerce or web applications cost more again. The only reliable number is a written quote against a written brief that lists pages, unique designs, functionality and content responsibilities.

### Why is one website quote five times higher than another?

Usually because the quotes cover different jobs: template versus custom design, a different number of unique page layouts, integrations such as CRM or booking, and who writes the content. Ask each designer to fill in the same scope table and the difference normally explains itself.

### Is a template-based website good enough for a small business?

Often yes. A clean, fast template-based site with proper SEO groundwork suits many small businesses. Custom design makes sense when the website has to differentiate your brand, support complex functionality or play a central role in winning clients.

### What costs come after the website is built?

Domain renewal, hosting, premium plugin or theme licences, maintenance and security updates, content changes and any marketing spend such as SEO or ads. Ask your designer to list recurring costs separately from the build price.

### Should I pay the whole amount upfront?

It is safer to tie payments to milestones such as design approval, development complete and launch. Staged payments keep both sides motivated and give you a clear point to review the work before the final payment.
